Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-boost-prompt-long-0081", "row_sha256": "cfbaa440d91a7f1348773320e45dc3048e6d368b88028d28efe7b15e57b2ac7c", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hi, could you turn this into a usable prompt for the person building the mercer family photo catalogue? it covers pictures from jan 1978 through dec 2004, not just the older albums. the working scans are in the shared folder called “Mercer Scans”; paper boxes are still in the hall closet and cousins are checking those separately, so the prompt should be about the scans and the inventory workbook, not ask anyone to move or sort the boxes. the workbook already has 214 rows, and some rows refer to the same picture in more than one scan. don't assume a row always equals a separate photograph. aunt elena's handwritten notes are in a folder named “Box A”, even though they mention pictures from several boxes. please use those notes as clues, not as proof when they disagree with a scan label.

we need a searchable spreadsheet for the family, plus a small public index that can be shared with the local history group. keep those as separate views, since not every record belongs in public. the spreadsheet should retain the current source ID and add columns for display title, date or date range, place, people named, source folder or note, duplicate link, visibility, and a short caption. use one row per distinct photograph in the finished working list; where two scan files are likely the same photograph, link the records in duplicate link rather than silently deleting a scan or counting it as two separate pictures. if it is not clear whether two files show the same photo, flag that for review and leave the link unset. don't add extra columns unless needed to explain a value already requested.

for dates, transcribe a date written on a scan or note exactly when it is legible, including a day and month if present. if the source only gives a year, enter the year; if it gives a range, keep the range. when a year is only an estimate, write “circa” before it and say which source suggested it in source folder or note. don't guess a date from clothing, cars, or the age of a person. if sources disagree, show both dates in the date field with a brief note about the disagreement, and don't pick one as certain. place should be the place stated on the scan or note, not a modern guess based on a building or landscape. if there is no place written down, leave that field blank rather than infer one.

names should come from a readable label, a note with a clear link to the image, or a family-confirmed identification already recorded in the workbook. a name mentioned in a general note isn't automatically the person in a photo. when it is uncertain who someone is, don't turn a question mark in the notes into a definite name; put “identity uncertain” in the caption only if that helps explain the source, and leave people named blank. keep spellings from the source, including nicknames, unless a family-confirmed spelling is in the workbook. don't expand initials by guessing. for a group photo, include only people who can be tied to the image by the sources, not everyone mentioned in the note.

1. visibility and the alternative branches: check whether a living person under 18 is identifiable in the image, including a child named in a caption or source note. if an identifiable living minor is shown, keep the photograph out of the public index and leave people named blank unless a dated guardian permission record is in the “Permissions” folder and can be matched to that photo. if the permission record is matched, the photo may go in the public index, but enter a minor's name only if the family has separately confirmed that name. the public/private mark doesn't override this rule for an identifiable living minor. otherwise, when no identifiable living minor is shown, use the scan's visibility mark: a “PUBLIC” mark means include it in the public index, while a “PRIVATE” mark means keep it in the family spreadsheet only. if neither mark appears, put the item in review and don't include it in the public index yet. at the delivery check, if a permission scan can't be matched to the photo's source ID, treat it as no matched permission and keep the photo out of the public index; don't assume that a nearby permission belongs to it. a review item can still be in the family spreadsheet.

captions should be short and factual, with a useful description of what the image shows and no invented occasion or relationship. if an actual family remark is useful, quote the words exactly and identify the person who said them only when the source does. one note says “we all squeezed in before the rain”; don't change that wording or make it sound like an established event. captions aren't a place to repeat every workbook note. keep spelling and punctuation ordinary, and don't add a quotation if the source doesn't contain one. use the short display title to distinguish photos for browsing, not to add a story that the records don't support.

please use the scan filename as the starting point for source ID and keep the original filename in the source folder or note field if the workbook doesn't already record it. don't rename files or alter scans. if the same photo exists as a color scan and a black-and-white scan, link them as duplicates only when the image itself supports that; note which versions they are in the caption or source field. keep the current workbook's IDs unchanged, including IDs attached to records you flag for review. the public index should contain only the records allowed by the visibility rules, and should carry the display title, date or date range, place when known, and caption. don't expose the family-only visibility or permission notes in that public index.

at the end, give the family a concise list of records that need review, stating the source ID and the specific unresolved issue, such as an unclear duplicate, disputed date, missing visibility mark, or uncertain identity. don't make a review note into a resolution. if something remains uncertain after checking the scans, workbook, and aunt elena's notes, keep the uncertainty visible in the family spreadsheet and leave the affected public-index entry out whenever the visibility rules require it. the period covered is still jan 1978 through dec 2004, and the paper boxes remain outside this task; keep the finished request focused on organizing the scanned catalogue and its two views.", "output": "Create a searchable catalogue of Mercer family photographs dated from January 1978 through December 2004. Work from the scans in the shared folder “Mercer Scans” and the existing inventory workbook, which has 214 rows. Paper boxes remain in the hall closet and are being checked separately: do not ask anyone to move or sort them. Some workbook rows may refer to the same photograph in more than one scan, so do not treat every row as a distinct picture. Aunt Elena’s handwritten notes are in “Box A” and may refer to images from several boxes. Use the notes as clues, not as proof when they conflict with a scan label.

Prepare two separate views: a searchable family spreadsheet and a smaller public index for the local history group. The family spreadsheet should retain each current source ID and include columns for display title, date or date range, place, people named, source folder or note, duplicate link, visibility, and a short caption. Use one row per distinct photograph in the finished working list. When two scan files are likely to show the same photograph, link the records in duplicate link rather than deleting a scan or counting two pictures. If it is unclear whether files show the same photograph, flag the issue for review and leave the link unset. Do not add columns unless they are needed to explain a value already requested.

For dates, transcribe a legible date from a scan or note exactly, including the day and month when present. Enter a year if that is all the source gives, and preserve a source’s date range. If a year is only an estimate, write “circa” before it and identify the source that suggested it in source folder or note. Do not estimate dates from clothing, cars, or a person’s age. If sources disagree, show both dates in the date field, briefly note the disagreement, and do not present either date as certain. Use the place stated on a scan or note; do not infer a modern location from a building or landscape. Leave place blank if no source states it.

Use names only when supported by a readable label, a note clearly linked to the image, or a family-confirmed identification already recorded in the workbook. A name in a general note does not by itself identify someone in a photograph. Do not turn a question mark in the notes into a definite name. If identity is uncertain, leave people named blank; use “identity uncertain” in the caption only when it helps explain the source. Retain source spellings, including nicknames, unless the workbook records a family-confirmed spelling. Do not expand initials by guessing. For group photographs, include only people the sources tie to the image, not everyone mentioned in a note.

1. Apply the visibility rules and keep both branches distinct:
   - If an identifiable living person under 18 is shown, including a child named in a caption or source note, keep the photograph out of the public index and leave people named blank unless a dated guardian permission record in “Permissions” can be matched to that photo. If a permission record is matched, the photo may be included in the public index, but enter a minor’s name only if the family has separately confirmed it. The scan’s public/private mark does not override this rule for an identifiable living minor.
   - Otherwise, when no identifiable living minor is shown, follow the scan’s visibility mark. A “PUBLIC” mark means include the photograph in the public index; a “PRIVATE” mark means keep it only in the family spreadsheet. If neither mark appears, put the item in review and do not include it in the public index yet. A review item may still appear in the family spreadsheet.

   At the delivery check, if a permission scan cannot be matched to the photograph’s source ID, treat it as no matched permission and keep the photograph out of the public index. Do not assume a nearby permission belongs to it.

Write short, factual captions that describe what the image shows without inventing an occasion or relationship. If a family remark is useful, quote its words exactly and identify the speaker only when the source does. One note says “we all squeezed in before the rain”; keep that wording unchanged and do not present it as an established event. Do not use captions to repeat every workbook note, add a quotation unsupported by the source, or turn a short display title into an unsupported story.

Use the scan filename as the starting point for source ID, and retain the original filename in source folder or note if it is not already recorded in the workbook. Do not rename files or alter scans. If the same photograph exists as a color scan and a black-and-white scan, link them as duplicates only when the image supports that identification; note which versions they are in the caption or source field. Keep current workbook IDs unchanged, including IDs for records flagged for review. Include in the public index only records allowed by the visibility rules. The public index should carry display title, date or date range, place when known, and caption; do not expose family-only visibility or permission notes there.

At the end, provide the family with a concise list of records needing review. For each, state the source ID and the specific unresolved issue, such as an unclear duplicate, disputed date, missing visibility mark, or uncertain identity. Do not turn a review note into a resolution. If uncertainty remains after checking the scans, workbook, and Aunt Elena’s notes, keep it visible in the family spreadsheet. Leave the affected public-index entry out whenever the visibility rules require it. Keep the request focused on organizing the scanned catalogue and its two views; the paper boxes remain outside this task, and the covered period remains January 1978 through December 2004."}]
